confidence_note: Verified in full text, ch. 10-11. The Oregon wine is Schwartz's own anecdote; no store or wine names. The depression figure is hedged in the book ('by some estimates'). The old quote about an 'expectation-outcome gap' is not verbatim and is dropped; social media is not in a 2004 book.
facts: On vacation in a tiny seaside town on the Oregon coast, Schwartz bought wine at a small grocery that had about a dozen options.
What he got wasn't very good, but he didn't expect very good, so he was satisfied.
In a store with hundreds or thousands of options his expectations would have been far higher, and the same bottle would have left him sorely disappointed.
He applies it to jeans: when they came in one variety he was satisfied with the fit; now he expects them to fit 'as though they were custom-made'.
Health: Americans live longer and healthier than ever, yet medical historian Roy Porter notes unparalleled anxiety about health.

By some estimates depression in 2000 was about ten times as likely as in 1900; depression among the Amish of Lancaster County is less than 20 percent of the national rate, a community with few life choices but expectations to match.
With limitless choice, people may get better results but feel worse, and often blame themselves.
His strategy 'Control Expectations': our evaluation of an experience depends on how it compares with what we expected; reduce the options you consider, be a satisficer, allow for serendipity.
scene_details: a small grocery on the Oregon coast with about a dozen wines
the same bottle imagined on a shelf of thousands
jeans expected to fit 'as though they were custom-made'
tension: The same mediocre bottle satisfies him in one shop and would have disappointed him in another.
opening_idea: Start with the not-very-good bottle from the dozen on the Oregon shelf and his satisfaction with it.

lessons.idea: Your satisfaction is measured against what you expected, so the size of the shelf shapes the expectation before you taste anything.
lessons.anchor: Same wine, a dozen options versus thousands.

reflect_final: Which recent choice disappointed you mostly because the wide range of options made you expect something close to perfect?

use_cases.situation: Partner disappointed by a restaurant after long research
use_cases.move: Schwartz says a mediocre wine from a dozen options satisfied him; suggest next time picking from a short list and seeing if the meal feels better.

use_cases.situation: Team frustrated a hire 'isn't perfect' after a huge candidate pool
use_cases.move: Ask what was actually expected for the role and whether the hire meets that.
Limit yourself to three options and leave one evening unplanned; notice how the unplanned evening feels.

pocket_idea: A shelf of thousands raises the bar before you taste; choose from fewer and the same wine can satisfy.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A not-very-good wine satisfied him because the shop only had a dozen.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Schwartz on the Oregon coast buys mediocre wine from a dozen options and is satisfied; in a store with thousands the same bottle would disappoint. Choice raises expectations; satisfaction is measured against them.
